findings.title: Substring matching applies error weights to non-error Discover queries
findings.body: Checking whether the raw query merely contains `event.type:error` does not establish that every selected event is an error. For example, `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` both satisfy this check (the endpoint itself demonstrates `!event.type:...` syntax), so an allowlisted Discover request rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count()`. This causes transaction/non-error rows to be counted with `sample_weight` even though the helper documents that transactions do not have that field, producing invalid counts or query failures. Determine eligibility from the parsed/effective query and require all query branches to be restricted to error events.

findings.title: Eligibility is checked against the outer dataset instead of the dataset being queried
findings.body: `_get_event_stats` executes queries against `scoped_dataset`, but this call passes the captured outer `dataset` into the upsampling predicate. In the dashboard split flow, an outer metrics-enhanced widget calls `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., errors_only_query, ...)`; the predicate sees the metrics dataset, returns false for it, and leaves the Discover error query as raw `count()`. Sampled errors in that dashboard path are therefore systematically undercounted. Evaluate eligibility against `scoped_dataset` (and the query actually passed to this invocation).

findings.title: Upsampled counts are truncated to integers
findings.body: The aggregate casts `sum(sample_weight)` through `toInt64`. Client sample rates are floats, so sample weights and their sums are not guaranteed to be integral (for example, a 0.3 sample rate produces a non-integral inverse weight). ClickHouse truncates this value before it reaches the API, creating a systematic low bias in the upsampled count. Preserve the numeric sum, or apply an explicitly chosen rounding policy only if the API contract requires integral results.

findings.title: The internal weighted aggregate is directly exposed to user queries
findings.body: `upsampled_count` is registered as a normal SnQL function and has no eligibility guard or `private=True` restriction. A caller can request `yAxis=upsampled_count()` directly, bypassing the allowlist and error-event checks in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`; this permits weighted counts for non-allowlisted projects and attempts to use `sample_weight` on transaction data. Keep this aggregate internal and/or enforce the same project and dataset eligibility at the resolver boundary.

findings.title: Process-randomized hash makes shared-cache keys and invalidation inconsistent
findings.body: Python's built-in `hash()` is salted per interpreter process. In a multi-worker deployment, the same organization/project selection produces different cache keys on different workers, so the shared cache does not actually share eligibility results. More importantly, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` running on one worker cannot delete entries created by another worker. Build the key from a stable serialized sorted project-ID list or a deterministic digest instead.
